key_terms.meaning: A drive that carries power through a belt, chain or rope which bends around pulleys or sprockets, allowing large shaft spacing and slight misalignment.
Both pulleys turn the same way and the belt does not cross itself; angle of lap on the small pulley is less than 180°.
The belt crosses over, so the pulleys turn in opposite directions and the lap angle exceeds 180° on both.
Loss of speed caused by unequal stretching of the belt on the tight and slack sides as it passes over the pulley.
Gross sliding between belt and rim when the load needs more friction than e<sup>μθ</sup> allows; unlike creep, it is avoided by design.
T<sub>c</sub> = m·v², where m = belt mass per metre (kg/m) and v = belt speed (m/s); it reduces the useful friction grip.
T = σbt, where σ = safe stress (N/mm²), b = belt width (mm), t = belt thickness (mm); the tight side must satisfy T₁ + T<sub>c</sub> ≤ T.
T₁/T₂ = e<sup>μθ</sup> for a flat belt, where T₁ = tight-side tension, T₂ = slack-side tension, μ = coefficient of friction, θ = angle of lap on the smaller pulley in radians.
The arc of pulley rim actually covered by the belt; for an open belt it is smaller on the small pulley, so that pulley sets the power limit.
P = (T₁ − T₂)·v, where T₁ and T₂ are in newtons and v = belt speed in m/s, giving P in watts.
T₀ = (T₁ + T₂)/2 + T<sub>c</sub>, the tension set when the belt is fitted.
The included angle of the V-groove, 34° to 38° (the belt itself is 40°); the belt wedges in and its two side reactions each lean at β to the groove centre line.
μ′ = μ/sin β, where β is the half groove angle; for β = 17–20° this is about three times the plain μ.
z = P<sub>d</sub>/(P<sub>r</sub>K<sub>θ</sub>K<sub>L</sub>), rounded up; V-drives are rated as a whole number of standard belts.
The rise and fall of each chain link as it travels as a chord of the sprocket polygon, giving a periodic speed fluctuation of the chain.
The distance between the centres of two adjacent rollers (mm); it fixes the chain size, the sprocket pitch circle and the load per link.
The tensile load at which the chain breaks; the chain pull must stay below it by a factor of safety, but the catalogue power rating, set by fatigue and wear, usually governs.
L = 2C/p + (Z₁ + Z₂)/2 + ((Z₂ − Z₁)/(2π))² p/C, rounded up to an even number of links.
The direction and pattern in which wires are twisted into strands and strands into rope: regular lay, lang lay, and right-hand or left-hand lay.
σ<sub>b</sub> = E<sub>r</sub>d<sub>w</sub>/D, where E<sub>r</sub> = rope modulus (about 0.8 × 10⁵ N/mm²), d<sub>w</sub> = outer wire diameter, D = sheave diameter.
Ratio of sheave diameter to rope diameter; at least about 30 for 6×19 and 18 for 6×37, larger for long life.
n = (F<sub>u</sub> − F<sub>b</sub>)/F<sub>t</sub>, with F<sub>t</sub> = (W + wl)(1 + a/g) and the bending load F<sub>b</sub> = σ<sub>b</sub>A.

takeaways: A flexible drive trades the rigid grip of gears for reach and tolerance of misalignment; what it costs is slip (belts), a lubrication need (chains) or bending fatigue (ropes).
The whole design of a flat belt comes from T₁/T₂ = e<sup>μθ</sup>, P = (T₁ − T₂)v and T₁ + T<sub>c</sub> ≤ σbt: friction fixes the tension ratio and strength fixes the width.
A V-belt multiplies friction by 1/sin β, roughly three times, so it can work with short centres and small pulleys; the price is that the drive is sold and rated in whole numbers of belts.
Chain drives give an exact velocity ratio because there is no slip, but chordal action, wear at the pin-bush hinge and the need for lubrication are built into the design.
Wire rope is a tension-only member; its strength is the sum of many small wires, and its life is decided as much by sheave diameter as by the breaking load.
Selecting any flexible element means comparing a design load (after service, duty and life factors) with a catalogue rating, then checking the strength condition with a factor of safety.
Misalignment, over-tensioning and under-tensioning cause most belt failures in the field; worn sprockets and dry pins cause most chain failures.

In a wire rope, bending stress repeats every time the rope passes over a sheave, so the factor of safety is counted after the bending load, the rope weight and the starting acceleration, not on the payload alone.
bank_note: Most syllabi that teach this unit ask for one belt, chain or rope design worked to numbers, and one derivation or comparison. Each long answer below has the points an examiner looks for, then a full model answer whose numbers are all worked out.

bank.q: Classify the flexible drives used for power transmission. Compare belts, chains and wire ropes on slip, velocity ratio, centre distance, lubrication and typical applications.
outline: Belts: flat, V, round and timing; friction drives (except timing belts) with creep and some slip, no lubrication
Chains: roller, silent, block and detachable; positive drive, exact mean ratio, need lubrication and alignment
Wire ropes: tension members wound on drums or run over sheaves, for hoisting over long lifts and spans
A comparison table on grip, slip, ratio, centre distance, shock, lubrication and use
All three allow distant shafts and some misalignment, which gears do not
answer: Definition: a flexible drive carries power between shafts through a member that bends round wheels on both shafts: a belt over pulleys, a chain over sprockets, or a rope over drums and sheaves. Nothing rigid joins the shafts, so they can be far apart and slightly out of line.

Belts. Flat belts grip one face by friction and need long centres to get enough arc of contact. V-belts wedge into grooves and grip on two sides, so they work on short centres with small pulleys. Round belts serve light drives such as sewing machines. Timing belts have teeth and do not slip. All friction belts show creep (a small, steady speed loss from elastic stretch) and slip under overload.

Chains. A roller chain has pins, bushes, rollers and inner and outer plates; the rollers seat in the sprocket teeth, so there is no slip and the mean velocity ratio is exactly Z₂/Z₁. Silent (inverted-tooth) chains run faster and quieter; block and detachable chains serve slow conveyors and farm machines. Chains need oil at the pin-bush hinge and show chordal speed variation.

Wire ropes. Steel wires twisted into strands and strands round a core make a strong, flexible tension member. Ropes do not transmit a speed ratio between two shafts: they lift or haul a load, wound on a drum and passed over sheaves. Their life depends on the sheave diameter as much as on the load.

answer.text: Comparison:

head: Feature
Flat belt
V-belt
Roller chain
Wire rope
rows: Tension; friction or winding on a drum

answer: Against gears: all three allow distant shafts and tolerate small misalignment, need no rigid casing, and are cheaper over long distances. Gears give an exact ratio in a small space but need accurate alignment, short centres and continuous lubrication.

Choosing among them: if some slip is acceptable and the shafts are far apart, a flat belt; for compact drives with shock, a V-belt; where the ratio must be exact or the drive is hot and oily, a chain; to lift or haul a load, a wire rope.

Check with numbers from the unit: a 15 kW flat belt at 15.08 m/s needs an 80 mm wide belt on 2 m centres; a 7.5 kW compressor needs 5 B-section V-belts on 420 mm centres; a 3 kW compressor runs on one strand of 08B chain at 503.4 mm centres; a 1000 kg goods hoist runs on an 11 mm 6×19 rope. The centre distances fall from metres to about half a metre as the grip becomes more positive.

bank.q: Discuss belt materials and belt construction. What properties must a belt material have, and how are flat belts joined into an endless loop?
outline: Materials: oak-tanned leather, rubber-bonded cotton duck, balata, nylon, polyester and aramid cords
Required properties: tensile strength, low stretch, high and steady friction, flexibility, resistance to moisture, oil and heat
Flat belt build: covers, fabric plies and cords near the neutral axis
Joints: cemented (skived), laced, hinged; joint efficiency reduces the allowable tension
V-belt build: tension cords under the top, rubber body, fabric wrap or raw edge
answer: Properties a belt material needs: high tensile strength to carry T₁ + T<sub>c</sub>; low stretch, so the tension set at fitting is kept; a high, steady coefficient of friction with the pulley; flexibility, so it bends over small pulleys without fatigue; low density, so the centrifugal tension m v² stays small; and resistance to moisture, oil, heat and abrasion.
Leather: oak-tanned hide, density about 1000 kg/m³, μ about 0.25 to 0.4 on cast iron. Strong and quiet, but it stretches with use, weakens when wet and needs dressing.

Rubber belts: plies of cotton duck (heavy woven canvas) bonded with rubber. The canvas carries the load and the rubber gives the friction face and the bond. Cheap, flexible and the common choice for general flat drives, but attacked by oil and heat.
Balata belts: cotton duck impregnated with balata gum; waterproof with high friction, but the gum softens above about 40 °C, so they suit cool, damp places.

Synthetic-cord belts: nylon (strong, absorbs shock, stretches), polyester (stiffer, holds length) or aramid (very strong, low stretch) cords in a rubber or polyurethane cover. They carry high power on narrow, fast belts.

Flat belt construction, outside to inside: a friction cover, fabric plies, the tension cords set as near as possible to the neutral axis, more plies and the inner cover. Cords at the neutral axis see almost no bending stress, so the belt survives small pulleys and many bends.

answer.text: Joining a flat belt into a loop:

head: Joint
How it is made
Comment
rows: Ends cut to a long taper, glued and pressed
Smooth, strongest, keeps most of the belt strength
Rubber ends cured together under heat
Endless, for rubber and synthetic belts
Rawhide or wire threaded through punched holes
Quick to fit, but heavier and weaker; slaps at each pulley
Quick to open; for temporary repairs

answer: Joint efficiency: the joint is the weakest section, so the safe tension σbt is multiplied by the joint efficiency (a laced joint loses more than a cemented one).

V-belt construction: moulded endless with a trapezoidal section. A layer of polyester or aramid tension cord lies just under the top face, with a rubber compression section below; the belt is fabric-wrapped, or raw-edged with exposed rubber sides for better grip. The belt’s included angle is 40° and the sections A to E run from 13 mm to 38 mm top width.

Check: the ideal material is strong, light and grippy. Leather’s 1000 kg/m³ gives T<sub>c</sub> = 135 N on a 100 mm × 6 mm belt at 15 m/s, but 540 N at 30 m/s, which is why fast drives move to lighter, stronger synthetic-cord belts.

bank.q: Derive the relation T₁/T₂ = e<sup>μθ</sup> for a flat belt drive and state the assumptions made. Show how it changes when centrifugal tension is included and for a V-belt.
outline: Element of belt subtending dθ with tensions T and T + dT
Radial balance dN = T dθ; tangential balance dT = μ dN
Integrate dT/T = μ dθ from T₂ to T₁: ln(T₁/T₂) = μθ
Assumptions: limiting friction over the whole arc, constant μ, thin inextensible belt, centrifugal effect neglected
With centrifugal tension: (T₁ − T<sub>c</sub>)/(T₂ − T<sub>c</sub>) = e<sup>μθ</sup> in total tensions; for a V-belt μ becomes μ/sin β
answer: Set-up: a belt on the driving pulley is about to slip. The tension rises from T₂ where the belt arrives to T₁ where it leaves, over the arc θ. Take a small piece of belt PQ that subtends the angle dθ at the pulley centre. The tension at P is T and at Q is T + dT. The rim pushes on the piece with a normal force dN and a friction force μ dN along the belt.

answer.text: Radial balance (along the line to the centre). Each end tension leans inward by dθ/2:
answer.pre:
dN = T sin(dθ/2) + (T + dT) sin(dθ/2)
   ≈ T dθ        (sin(dθ/2) ≈ dθ/2, and dT × dθ is negligible)

answer.text: Tangential balance (along the belt). The tension difference is carried by friction:
answer.pre:
(T + dT) cos(dθ/2) − T cos(dθ/2) = μ dN
dT = μ T dθ      (cos(dθ/2) ≈ 1)

answer.text: Separate and integrate over the arc of contact:
answer.pre:
dT / T = μ dθ
∫ from T₂ to T₁ of dT/T = μ ∫ from 0 to θ of dθ
ln(T₁/T₂) = μθ
T₁/T₂ = exp(μθ)

answer: Assumptions: the belt is on the point of slipping over the whole arc, so friction is at its limit everywhere; μ is constant; the belt is thin and does not stretch; the belt’s mass is neglected (no centrifugal force); θ is in radians and is the arc of the pulley that slips first, the smaller pulley of an open drive.

answer.text: With centrifugal tension. A moving piece of mass m dθ r and speed v needs an inward force m v² dθ; this is supplied by the tension itself, so it does not press the belt on the rim. The radial balance becomes:
answer.pre:
dN = (T − m v²) dθ = (T − T<sub>c</sub>) dθ
dT = μ (T − T<sub>c</sub>) dθ
ln[(T₁ − T<sub>c</sub>)/(T₂ − T<sub>c</sub>)] = μθ

answer: Here T₁ and T₂ are the total tensions. If, as in the design chapters, T₁ and T₂ denote the friction tensions only, then the total tight-side pull is T₁ + T<sub>c</sub> and the simple form T₁/T₂ = e<sup>μθ</sup> still holds for them.

V-belt: the radial push R on the belt is balanced by two side reactions R<sub>n</sub> that lean at β, so 2R<sub>n</sub> sin β = R and the friction is 2μR<sub>n</sub> = μR/sin β. Replacing μ by μ/sin β in the derivation gives T₁/T₂ = e<sup>μθ/sin β</sup>.

Check with numbers: for μ = 0.3 and θ = 168.52° = 2.941 rad, e<sup>0.8824</sup> = 2.417, the ratio of the flat-belt worked example. A V-groove of 38° (β = 19°) with μ = 0.2 on the 2.462 rad arc of the V-belt example gives e<sup>1.512</sup> = 4.54 against 1.64 for a flat rim. If θ were used in degrees, 0.3 × 168.52 = 50.6 would give an impossible ratio of about 10²².

bank.q: Explain chordal action in a chain drive. What are its effects and how are they reduced in design?
outline: The chain wraps the sprocket as a polygon; each link is a chord of the pitch circle
Link speed varies between πdN/60 × cos(180°/Z) and πdN/60; fractional variation 1 − cos(180°/Z)
The chain line also rises and falls by (d/2)(1 − cos(180°/Z))
Effects: speed pulsation, impact at engagement, vibration, noise, wear and extra dynamic load
Remedies: more teeth (at least 17, 19 for smooth running), smaller pitch, moderate speed, guides or idlers
answer: Cause: a chain cannot bend between its pins, so on the sprocket it lies as a polygon whose sides are the links. The roller centres lie on the pitch circle d = p/sin(180°/Z), and each link is a chord that subtends 360°/Z at the centre.

Speed variation: the sprocket turns at a steady speed N, but the chain leaving it moves at the horizontal speed of the roller that is just leaving. When that roller is at the top of the pitch circle its speed is v<sub>max</sub> = πdN/60; half a tooth later the link is tilted by 180°/Z and the horizontal speed falls to v<sub>min</sub> = v<sub>max</sub> cos(180°/Z). The fractional speed variation is 1 − cos(180°/Z).
Rise and fall: the chain line also moves up and down. The leaving point swings between the full pitch radius d/2 and (d/2)cos(180°/Z), a movement of (d/2)(1 − cos(180°/Z)).

answer.text: Numbers for 08B chain (p = 12.7 mm):

answer: Effects: the driven sprocket receives a pulsating speed, so the chain and the shafts see a fluctuating load at the tooth frequency; each roller hits the tooth as it enters, which causes noise, impact fatigue of rollers and bushes, and wear; at high speed the pulsation can excite vibration of the chain span.
Effect of few teeth: a small Z gives a large variation and also a small pitch diameter, so the same torque needs a larger chain pull F = 2T/d. Both hurt chain life.

Reducing chordal action in design: (1) use enough teeth on the small sprocket, at least 17 and 19 or more for smooth running; (2) use a smaller pitch (several strands of a small pitch rather than one large-pitch strand); (3) keep the speed moderate for the pitch chosen, as the rating charts do; (4) choose a centre distance that avoids span resonance, and use guides or an idler on long spans; (5) keep the chain lubricated so impact and wear stay low.
Silent chains and toothed belts are used where even this small pulsation matters, for example camshaft drives.
Check: the worked example’s 19-tooth sprocket at 1000 rpm gives link speeds between 4.040 and 3.985 m/s, a 1.36 % swing, and its mean speed Z₁pN₁/60 = 4.022 m/s lies between them, as it must.

bank.q: Describe the construction of a wire rope and explain regular lay, lang lay, and right-hand and left-hand lay, with the use of each.
outline: Wires twisted into strands, strands laid round a fibre core or IWRC
Designation 6×19: 6 strands of 19 wires (12 outer, 6 inner, 1 centre); 6×7, 6×37, 8×19 and their uses
Regular lay: wires opposite to strands; stable, resists crushing and rotation
Lang lay: wires and strands the same way; flexible, wears longer, but untwists; ends must be fixed
Right-hand and left-hand lay describe the strand helix; lay length; lay matched to the drum grooving
answer: Construction: steel wires are twisted into strands, and the strands are laid in a helix round a core. The core supports the strands and keeps the rope round. A fibre core (sisal, manila or polypropylene) holds lubricant and gives flexibility; an independent wire rope core (IWRC), itself a small rope, adds strength and resists crushing on the drum and heat.

Designation: 6×19 means 6 strands with 19 wires in each. A standard 6×19 strand has 1 centre wire, 6 inner wires and 12 outer wires. Fewer, thicker wires resist abrasion and are stiff; more, finer wires are flexible but wear faster.

answer.text: Common constructions:

head: Rope
Character
Use
Smallest sheave, about
rows: Stiff, coarse wires, good abrasion resistance

answer: Regular (cross) lay: the wires in each strand are twisted opposite to the direction in which the strands are laid round the core. The outer wires lie roughly along the rope axis. The rope is stable, resists crushing and kinking, and a free load does not spin much. It is the default for cranes and single-fall hoists.

Lang lay: the wires and the strands are twisted the same way, so the outer wires cross the rope at an angle and a longer length of each wire touches the sheave. It is more flexible and wears longer, but the two twists add, so under load it tends to untwist and spin a free load. Use it only where both ends are fixed or the load is guided, as in mine shafts, excavators and haulage.

Right-hand and left-hand lay: these name the direction of the strand helix. Hold the rope vertical; if the strands climb to the right like an ordinary screw thread, it is right-hand lay; otherwise left-hand. Right-hand regular lay is the usual stock rope. The lay direction is matched to the drum grooving so that winding does not unlay the rope.

Lay length: the length of rope in which one strand makes one full turn, about six to seven rope diameters in ordinary ropes. Order a rope by diameter, construction, core, lay type and direction, and grade.
Other forms: spiral strand and locked coil ropes, made of layers of wires with no separate strands, give a smooth closed surface for standing duty such as bridge stays and guys.

Check: a 6×19 rope has 6 × 19 = 114 wires. In the goods-hoist example its outer wires are about d/15 = 0.73 mm across on an 11 mm rope, which is why the bending stress σ<sub>b</sub> = E<sub>r</sub>d<sub>w</sub>/D stays at 117.3 N/mm² on a 500 mm sheave.

bank.q: A flat belt transmits 15 kW at a belt speed of 15 m/s between pulleys of 300 mm and 900 mm diameter on a centre distance of 2.5 m (open drive). μ = 0.3, the safe stress in the belt is 2.5 N/mm², the belt is 10 mm thick and its density is 1000 kg/m³. Find the belt width, choose a standard width, and find the initial tension and the belt length.
outline: Arc on the small pulley θ = 180° − 2 sin⁻¹((D − d)/(2C)) in radians
T₁ − T₂ = P/v and T₁/T₂ = e<sup>μθ</sup>
T<sub>c</sub> = m v² with m = ρbt
T₁ + T<sub>c</sub> = σbt gives b; round up and check the stress
T₀ = (T₁ + T₂)/2 + T<sub>c</sub>; open-belt length

answer.text: Arc of contact on the small pulley:

answer: Tension ratio: μθ = 0.3 × 2.901 = 0.8703, so T₁/T₂ = e<sup>0.8703</sup> = 2.388.

answer.text: Tensions from the power:

answer: Centrifugal tension per millimetre of width: m = ρ × (b/1000) × 0.010 = 0.010b kg/m (b in mm), so T<sub>c</sub> = 0.010b × 15² = 2.25b N.

answer.text: Strength condition, with σbt = 2.5 × b × 10 = 25b N:
Choose the next standard width and check it:

answer: Adopt b = 80 mm. Its centrifugal tension is m v² = 0.8 × 15² = 180 N.

answer.text: Belt length of the open drive:

answer: Speeds that go with the data: the small pulley turns at N = 60v/(πd) = 60 × 15/(π × 0.3) = 954.9 rpm and the large one at 318.3 rpm, a 3 : 1 ratio, ignoring slip.
Pulley face: make it about a quarter wider than the belt, about 100 mm.

Speed margin: this 80 mm belt has a safe tension T = 25 × 80 = 2000 N and m = 0.8 kg/m, so its maximum-power speed is v = √(T/(3m)) = √(2000/2.4) = 28.9 m/s. Running at 15 m/s is well below that, so raising the speed a little would still increase the power it can carry, while centrifugal tension takes only 180 N of the 2000 N now.

Check: power from the final tensions, (1720.6 − 720.6) × 15 = 15 000 W, as required; the ratio 1720.6/720.6 = 2.388 = e<sup>0.8703</sup>; and the 80 mm belt works at 2.38 N/mm², just inside 2.5 N/mm². Leaving out T<sub>c</sub> would have given b = 1720.6/25 = 68.8 mm, too narrow.

bank.q: A V-belt drive transmits 20 kW from a 1440 rpm motor to a compressor at 480 rpm. The small pulley has a pitch diameter of 200 mm and the centre distance is 800 mm. The groove angle is 38°, μ = 0.25, each C-section belt weighs 0.30 kg/m and may carry a safe tension of 800 N, and the service factor is 1.2. Find the number of belts and the belt length.
outline: D = 600 mm from the speed ratio; v = πdN/60
Arc on the small pulley θ = 180° − 2 sin⁻¹((D − d)/(2C))
Effective friction μ/sin β and the ratio e<sup>μθ/sin β</sup>
Per belt: T₁ = safe tension − T<sub>c</sub>, T₂ = T₁/ratio, P = (T₁ − T₂)v
Design power with the service factor; number of belts rounded up; pitch length
answer: Data: P = 20 kW, N₁ = 1440 rpm, N₂ = 480 rpm, d = 0.200 m, C = 0.800 m, 2β = 38°, μ = 0.25, m = 0.30 kg/m, safe tension 800 N per belt, service factor 1.2.
Large pulley: speed ratio 1440/480 = 3, so D = 3 × 200 = 600 mm.
Belt speed: v = πdN₁/60 = π × 0.200 × 1440/60 = 15.08 m/s, inside the usual limit for V-belts.

answer.text: Arc of contact on the small pulley:
Tension ratio with the wedge:

answer: Centrifugal tension: T<sub>c</sub> = m v² = 0.30 × 15.08² = 68.2 N.

answer.text: Power one belt can carry:

answer: Design power: P<sub>d</sub> = 1.2 × 20 = 24 kW.

Number of belts: z = 24/9.58 = 2.51, so use 3 belts. Each then carries 24 000/(3 × 15.08) = 530.5 N of tension difference, so T₁ = 530.5 × 7.57/6.57 = 611.3 N and the tight-side pull is 611.3 + 68.2 = 679.5 N, below 800 N.

answer.text: Pitch length:

answer: Order the nearest standard C-section pitch length from the maker’s list and set the centre distance to suit it.

Large pulley: its arc is 180° + 28.96° = 208.96°, larger than the small pulley’s, so the small pulley slips first and was rightly used. Shaft load, roughly the sum of the friction tensions of the three belts (centrifugal tension does not press on the shaft): 3 × (611.3 + 80.7) = 3 × 692.0 = 2076 N, which the shaft and bearing design must carry.
Comparison: a flat belt with the same μ on the same arc has e<sup>0.659</sup> = 1.93 instead of 7.57, so the wedge is what lets three belts do the work on short 800 mm centres.

Check: 3 belts × 9.58 kW = 28.7 kW ≥ 24 kW; the speed ratio 600/200 = 3 matches 1440/480; and the tight-side pull of 679.5 N leaves a margin under the 800 N safe tension. In a design office the count would also be checked against the maker’s rating chart, which allows for fatigue life.

bank.q: Design a roller chain drive to transmit 10 kW from a small sprocket at 1000 rpm to a machine at 400 rpm, with a service factor of 1.3. The maker’s chart rates one strand of 12B chain (p = 19.05 mm, breaking load 28.9 kN) at 14 kW at 1000 rpm on a 20-tooth sprocket. Use a centre distance of about 40 pitches. Give the sprockets, chain length, exact centre distance, factor of safety and lubrication.
outline: Speed ratio 2.5: Z₁ = 20, Z₂ = 50
Design power 13 kW against the 14 kW rating: one strand of 12B
Pitch diameters d = p/sin(180°/Z); mean speed v = Z₁pN₁/60; chain pull and factor of safety
Length in pitches, rounded up to even links; exact centre distance
Speed variation, sag and the lubrication method
answer: Data: P = 10 kW, N₁ = 1000 rpm, N₂ = 400 rpm, K<sub>s</sub> = 1.3, 12B chain with p = 19.05 mm and breaking load 28.9 kN, rated 14 kW per strand at 1000 rpm on 20 teeth.
Teeth: the speed ratio is 1000/400 = 2.5. Take Z₁ = 20 (above the 19-tooth smooth-running minimum) and Z₂ = 2.5 × 20 = 50. The machine then runs at exactly 400 rpm.
Chain choice: design power = 1.3 × 10 = 13 kW. One strand of 12B is rated at 14 kW, which is more than 13 kW, so a single-strand 12B chain is selected.

answer.text: Pitch diameters:

answer: Mean chain speed: v = Z₁pN₁/60 = 20 × 0.01905 × 1000/60 = 6.350 m/s.
Chain pull: F = P/v = 10 000/6.350 = 1574.8 N. Factor of safety on breaking load = 28 900/1574.8 = 18.4, so the chain is in no danger of breaking; the power rating governs.

answer.text: Chain length for C = 40p = 762 mm:
Exact centre distance for 116 links:

answer: Chain length: 116 × 19.05 = 2209.8 mm.
Speed variation: 1 − cos(180°/20) = 1 − cos 9° = 0.0123, or 1.23 %, small enough for a machine drive.
Sag and adjustment: leave a slack-side sag of about 2 % of C, 0.02 × 766.1 = 15 mm, and mount the motor or one sprocket on an adjustable base, or fit an idler, to take up wear.
Lubrication: at 6.35 m/s and 10 kW the chain should run in a closed case with an oil bath or a slinger disc, so that oil reaches every pin-bush hinge; manual or drip oiling is for slower drives.

answer: Check: v = πd₁N₁/60 = π × 0.12178 × 1000/60 = 6.376 m/s at the pitch circle, 0.4 % above the 6.350 m/s mean speed, as expected for 20 teeth; and 116 links put the shafts 4.1 mm further apart than the 762 mm first chosen, because the length was rounded up.

bank.q: A wire rope hoist lifts a load of 20 kN through 40 m, accelerating at 0.5 m/s² when it starts. The sheave diameter is 25 times the rope diameter. Use a 6×19 fibre-core rope with ultimate stress 1600 N/mm² on its metallic area, A = 0.4d², d<sub>w</sub> = d/15, E<sub>r</sub> = 0.8 × 10⁵ N/mm² and mass 0.0037d² kg/m (d in mm). Select the rope diameter for a factor of safety of 5 with bending counted, and comment on the sheave.
outline: Choose 6×19 fibre core, regular lay, for a general hoist
Bending stress σ<sub>b</sub> = E<sub>r</sub>d<sub>w</sub>/D does not depend on d when D/d is fixed
F<sub>t</sub> = (W + wl)(1 + a/g); F<sub>b</sub> = σ<sub>b</sub>A; n = (F<sub>u</sub> − F<sub>b</sub>)/F<sub>t</sub>
Solve for d, round to a standard size, recheck n
D/d = 25 is below the 30 usually asked for 6×19: a larger sheave raises n and life
answer: Rope type: a general hoist with a free load takes 6×19 with a fibre core in right-hand regular lay, which does not spin the load.
Bending stress: with D = 25d and d<sub>w</sub> = d/15, σ<sub>b</sub> = E<sub>r</sub>d<sub>w</sub>/D = 0.8 × 10⁵ × (d/15)/(25d) = 0.8 × 10⁵/375 = 213.3 N/mm², the same for every rope size.
First estimate from the load alone: F<sub>u</sub> = 5 × 20 000 = 100 000 N = 1600 × 0.4d², so d = √(100 000/640) = 12.5 mm. Bending and acceleration will need more.

answer.text: Solve for the diameter that gives n = 5 with everything counted (all forces in N, d in mm):

answer: Adopt the next standard size, d = 14 mm.

answer.text: Check the 14 mm rope:
Effect of rope size (D = 25d):

answer: Sheave: D = 25 × 14 = 350 mm. This is below the 30d (420 mm) that 6×19 rope normally needs, so the rope would fail early in fatigue. With a 420 mm sheave, σ<sub>b</sub> = 0.8 × 10⁵ × 0.933/420 = 177.8 N/mm², F<sub>b</sub> = 13 938 N and n = (125 440 − 13 938)/21 318 = 5.23. The better design keeps the 14 mm rope and raises the sheave to at least 420 mm.
Alternative: a 6×37 rope (finer wires, sheaves down to about 18d) could stay on the 350 mm sheave, but its area coefficient and wire size differ, so it must be recalculated.
Check: the static factor 125 440/20 000 = 6.27 drops to 5.10 once the 16.7 kN bending load and the 1.0 kN starting load are counted, which is why a hoist rope is never sized on the payload alone.

bank.q: Explain step by step how the length of an open belt between two pulleys of diameters d and D at centre distance C is found, and how the same geometry gives the angle of lap. Work it for d = 200 mm, D = 600 mm and C = 2 m, and compare a crossed belt.
outline: Geometry: the straight spans are tangents; sin α = (D − d)/(2C)
Arc on the small pulley π − 2α, on the large pulley π + 2α
Exact length = 2C cos α + (D/2)(π + 2α) + (d/2)(π − 2α); approximation L = 2C + π(D + d)/2 + (D − d)²/(4C)
Crossed belt: sin α = (D + d)/(2C), lap π + 2α on both, L = 2C + π(D + d)/2 + (D + d)²/(4C)
The smaller lap sets e<sup>μθ</sup>; a small lap makes the drive slip
answer: Geometry: draw the two pulleys with centres O₁ (small, radius r = d/2) and O₂ (large, radius R = D/2), a distance C apart. Each straight span of belt is a common tangent. Drop a line from O₁ parallel to the span; it meets the radius of O₂ at a point R − r from the rim, so the span makes an angle α with the line of centres, where sin α = (R − r)/C = (D − d)/(2C).
Angle of lap: the belt leaves the small pulley α before the line of centres on each side, so it wraps θ<sub>s</sub> = π − 2α. On the large pulley it wraps θ<sub>L</sub> = π + 2α.

answer.text: Length: two straight spans plus the two arcs.
answer.pre:
each span = C cos α
L = 2C cos α + R(π + 2α) + r(π − 2α)
  = 2C cos α + π(R + r) + 2α(R − r)

answer: Approximation: for small α, cos α ≈ 1 − α²/2 and α ≈ (R − r)/C. Substituting gives L ≈ 2C + π(R + r) + (R − r)²/C, that is L = 2C + π(D + d)/2 + (D − d)²/(4C).

answer.text: Numbers for d = 200 mm, D = 600 mm, C = 2000 mm:

answer: Crossed belt: the spans cross between the pulleys, so sin α = (R + r)/C = (D + d)/(2C) and the belt wraps π + 2α on both pulleys. Its length is L = 2C + π(D + d)/2 + (D + d)²/(4C).

answer.text: Crossed belt with the same numbers:

answer: Use in design: the smaller arc goes into the tension ratio e<sup>μθ</sup> because that pulley slips first. For the open drive θ = 168.52° = 2.941 rad; the crossed drive’s 203.07° grips better but the belt rubs where it crosses and the shafts turn opposite ways. A short centre distance with a large speed ratio shrinks the small-pulley arc and the grip; then increase C or add an idler that wraps the belt further round.
Check: the approximate and exact open lengths differ by only 0.1 mm here, and the crossed belt is 60 mm longer because (D + d)² − (D − d)² = 4Dd, and 4 × 600 × 200/(4 × 2000) = 60 mm.

bank.q: For a given duty, compare flat belt, V-belt and chain drives and justify which one you would choose where the centre distance is short, the speed ratio is high and no slip can be tolerated.
outline: Flat belt: needs long centres and a large arc; slips; poor for high ratios
V-belt: wedge gives μ/sin β, works on short centres, but still a friction drive with creep
Chain: positive drive, exact mean ratio, short centres, high ratios with enough teeth
Recommend the chain (or a timing belt at light load); state the costs: lubrication, alignment, chordal action
Support with numbers for the arc and the tension ratio
answer: The duty sets three tests: short centres, a high ratio, and no slip. A high ratio on short centres makes the arc of contact on the small pulley small, so any friction drive loses grip just where it needs it most.

answer.text: Effect of a high ratio on short centres. Take d = 100 mm, D = 500 mm (ratio 5) and C = 500 mm:
Grip that this arc gives with μ = 0.25:

head: Drive
Exponent
T₁/T₂
Share of T₁ that drives, 1 − T₂/T₁

answer: Flat belt: on 132.84° of arc it can turn only 44 % of its tight-side tension into driving force, so it needs a wide belt and high shaft loads; it also creeps and slips. It fails the short-centre and no-slip tests.

V-belt: the wedge raises the ratio to 5.93, so it works well on short centres and high ratios; this is why V-drives dominate compact industrial drives. But it still creeps and slips on overload, so it fails the no-slip test.

Chain: the rollers seat in the teeth, so the mean ratio is exactly Z₂/Z₁ with no creep or slip. A ratio of 5 needs, for example, Z₁ = 19 and Z₂ = 95; the short centre distance is fine because a chain needs only enough wrap to engage a few teeth. It passes all three tests.

Costs of the chain: it needs lubrication of the pin-bush hinge and a closed case at speed, accurate alignment of the sprockets, and it pulsates by 1 − cos(180°/Z₁), 1.36 % at 19 teeth. Very high ratios with a small sprocket also wrap few teeth, so ratios above about 6 to 7 in one stage are usually split into two.
Alternative: a timing belt is also positive, clean and quiet, and suits light to moderate power at high speed; a chain is preferred at high torque, in heat or in dirt.
Recommendation: a roller chain drive (or a timing belt if the load is light and the place must stay clean), with Z₁ of at least 17 to 19, an even number of links and proper lubrication.

Check: the table’s numbers follow from 0.25 × 2.318 = 0.580 and 0.25/0.3256 × 2.318 = 1.780; e<sup>0.580</sup> = 1.79 and e<sup>1.780</sup> = 5.93. The V-belt’s advantage is real, but only the chain removes slip entirely.

bank.q: Explain why replacing a flat pulley by a V-grooved pulley greatly increases the power that can be carried for the same belt tension, and discuss the side effects of that change on the drive.
outline: Wedge: 2R<sub>n</sub> sin β = R, friction μR/sin β, so the exponent becomes μθ/sin β
Numbers: β = 19°, 1/sin β = 3.07; the ratio rises from 2.09 to 9.57 for μ = 0.25, θ = 2.94 rad
Same T₁ carries more power, or the same power needs a smaller T₂ and lower shaft load
Side effects: thicker belt needs larger minimum pulleys; heat and loss from wedging; groove wear; matched sets
Conclusion on when the V-groove is worth it
answer: Mechanism: on a flat rim the radial push R of the belt equals the normal force, and friction is μR. In a groove of half angle β, the belt touches two sloping flanks. Each pushes back with R<sub>n</sub>, and only their radial parts balance R: 2R<sub>n</sub> sin β = R. Friction acts on both flanks, so it is 2μR<sub>n</sub> = μR/sin β. The derivation of the tension ratio is unchanged except that μ becomes μ′ = μ/sin β, giving T₁/T₂ = e<sup>μθ/sin β</sup>.
Size of the gain: for the usual 38° groove, β = 19° and 1/sin β = 3.07, so the exponent is three times larger. Because the ratio is an exponential, the tension ratio grows far more than three times.

answer.text: Numbers, μ = 0.25 and θ = 168.52° = 2.941 rad:
answer.pre:
flat:   T₁/T₂ = exp(0.25 × 2.941) = exp(0.735) = 2.09
V:      T₁/T₂ = exp(0.768 × 2.941) = exp(2.258) = 9.57
share of T₁ that drives, 1 − T₂/T₁:   flat 0.521,  V 0.895

answer: Same tension, more power: power is P = T₁(1 − T₂/T₁)v, so for the same safe T₁ and speed the V-groove carries 0.895/0.521 = 1.72 times the power of the flat rim.

answer.text: Same power, lower shaft load. For 10 kW at 15 m/s, T₁ − T₂ = 666.7 N:

head: Pulley
T₂ (N)
T₁ (N)
T₁ + T₂ (N), roughly the shaft load

answer: So the V-drive does not load the bearings more for the same power; it needs less initial tension and gives a smaller shaft load. The large wedge forces R<sub>n</sub> act inside the pulley rim, not on the shaft.

Side effects that do matter: (1) the V-belt is thick, so it bends harder and needs larger minimum pulley diameters for each section; (2) the belt is wedged in and pulled out of the groove at every turn, which costs some efficiency and heats the belt; (3) the flanks wear, and a worn groove lets the belt bottom, which kills the wedge; (4) one belt carries only a few kilowatts, so drives use several belts, which must be a matched set tensioned together; (5) the groove angle must suit the pulley size (34° to 38°) so the bent belt still bears on both sides.
Conclusion: the V-groove is worth it whenever centres are short or the ratio is high, because it multiplies the usable grip at the cost of a thicker, lossier belt and grooves that must be kept true.
Check: 1/sin 19° = 1/0.3256 = 3.07, 0.25 × 3.07 = 0.768, and 666.7 × 2.086/(2.086 − 1) = 1280.5 N for the flat rim, as in the table (2.086 is the unrounded ratio).

bank.q: A wire rope fails repeatedly in service at the same place near a sheave. Analyse the likely causes and explain how tension, bending, sheave size and lay each affect rope life.
outline: Bending fatigue at the sheave: σ<sub>b</sub> = E<sub>r</sub>d<sub>w</sub>/D; a small sheave is the first suspect
Tension: rope weight and starting acceleration raise F<sub>t</sub>; n = (F<sub>u</sub> − F<sub>b</sub>)/F<sub>t</sub>
Sheave and groove: D/d, groove radius, reverse bends, fleet angle
Lay and construction: regular vs lang lay, 6×19 vs 6×37, core crushing
Other causes: dry or corroded rope, shock from slack rope, damaged sheave; remedies
answer: Reading the symptom: failure at the same place near a sheave points to the length of rope that bends over that sheave most often, under the highest tension, for example the part that sits on the sheave when the load starts to lift. Broken outer wires there are the classic sign of bending fatigue.

Bending: each pass over a sheave bends the outer wires to the sheave radius, with σ<sub>b</sub> = E<sub>r</sub>d<sub>w</sub>/D, and straightens them again: one stress cycle per pass. Take the goods-hoist rope of the worked example (11 mm, 6×19, d<sub>w</sub> = 0.733 mm, A = 48.4 mm², F<sub>u</sub> = 67 760 N, F<sub>t</sub> = 10 956 N).

answer.text: Effect of the sheave diameter on that rope:

answer: A 300 mm guide sheave on the same rope raises the bending stress by two thirds and drops below the 30d minimum for 6×19. The static factor barely changes, but fatigue life falls steeply, so a small sheave is the first suspect. A sheave that bends the rope the opposite way (a reverse bend) does even more harm, because each pass gives a full reversal.

Tension: the steady tension adds to the bending stress in every wire. Starting acceleration, rope weight on a long lift and any shock when slack rope is snatched tight raise the peak pull F<sub>t</sub>. In the example the starting pull is 10 956 N against 9810 N of payload, an extra 11.7 %.

Sheave groove: a groove that is too narrow pinches and flattens the rope; one that is too wide lets it flatten under load; a worn, corrugated groove scores the wires. A large fleet angle (the rope running onto the sheave at a slant) rubs the rope against the flange. All of these concentrate wear on the length that runs over that sheave.

Lay and construction: lang lay puts a longer length of each outer wire on the sheave and resists bending fatigue and wear better, but it must have both ends fixed. A more flexible construction (6×37, with wires about d/22) lowers σ<sub>b</sub> for the same sheave. A fibre core can be crushed on a small sheave or a drum, letting the strands bite into each other; an IWRC resists that.
Other causes: dry rope (the wires rub and fret inside), corrosion from water or acid fumes, kinks from bad handling, and a seized sheave bearing that drags the rope.

Remedies, in order of effect: (1) enlarge the sheave to at least 30d for 6×19, better 45d; (2) remove reverse bends; (3) correct the groove size and fleet angle; (4) consider a more flexible construction or lang lay where both ends are fixed; (5) start smoothly with the rope taut; (6) keep the rope dressed and inspect that length for broken wires.

bank.q: Discuss the modes of failure of a roller chain drive and explain how lubrication and the number of sprocket teeth influence each mode.
outline: Link plate fatigue under fluctuating tension
Roller and bush impact fatigue at engagement
Pin and bush wear: pitch elongation, riding up and jumping teeth
Galling of the pin-bush hinge; sprocket tooth wear
Lubrication methods by speed, and the effect of tooth count through chordal action and chain pull
answer: A chain is a string of hinges loaded in tension. Its failures come from the fluctuating pull, from the impact of each roller on the tooth, and from sliding in the hinges.

Link plate fatigue: the pull rises from near zero on the slack side to full tension on the tight side once per circuit of the chain, so the plates see a fluctuating tensile stress and crack at the holes. This mode limits the rating at low and medium speed.
Roller and bush impact fatigue: each roller strikes a tooth as it enters the sprocket. The impact grows with speed and pitch and with fewer teeth, so this mode limits the rating at high speed.

Pin and bush wear: the pin turns inside the bush under load each time the link enters and leaves a sprocket. Wear there lengthens every pitch, so the chain rides higher on the teeth and finally jumps them. Makers set the replacement limit at about 1.5 % to 3 % elongation.
Galling: at high speed and load the oil film in the hinge breaks down, the pin and bush weld and tear, and the chain seizes quickly.
Sprocket tooth wear: a stretched chain bears on the tip side of the teeth and hooks them, and a worn sprocket in turn wears a new chain fast, so chain and sprockets are replaced together.

answer.text: Effect of lubrication:

head: Mode
What oil does
rows: Separates the sliding surfaces; the main defence, wear rises steeply when dry
Keeps the film unbroken; needs a continuous supply at high speed
Cushions the roller on the tooth and reduces noise
Little direct effect, but prevents fretting and corrosion that start cracks

answer: Lubrication methods rise with speed: manual or brush oiling for slow drives, drip feed, an oil bath or slinger disc in a closed case, and a pressure spray for high speed. Oil must reach the pin-bush gap, so it is fed onto the inner edges of the link plates on the slack side.

answer.text: Effect of the number of teeth on the small sprocket (08B chain, 3 kW at 1000 rpm):

answer: Few teeth raise both the impact and the chain pull: the 11-tooth sprocket gives three times the speed pulsation and 71 % more pull than the 19-tooth one, and each link also turns through a larger angle (360°/Z) in the hinge, so wear per engagement rises. Hence at least 17 teeth, and 19 or more for smooth running.

bank.q: A plant must choose between a chain drive and a V-belt drive for a crusher that has heavy starting torque and shock. Evaluate both options and recommend one with reasons.
outline: Crusher duty: shock, overload, jamming, dust; the drive should protect the machine and motor
V-belt: elastic, damps shock, slips on a jam (a mechanical fuse), no lubrication, tolerant of dust
Chain: positive, passes shock to shafts and bearings, needs oil and a sealed case in dust, exact ratio not needed
Design consequences: service factor about 1.5 or more, number of belts, shaft loads
Recommend the V-belt drive and state when the chain would be chosen instead
answer: What the crusher duty demands: a jaw or cone crusher starts under heavy load, takes repeated shocks as rock breaks, and can jam outright. The drive should start the machine, survive the shocks, and protect the motor and the shafts when it jams. Dust is everywhere. An exact speed ratio is not needed.

V-belt drive: rubber belts are elastic, so each shock is softened before it reaches the motor. On a jam the belts slip and squeal instead of breaking a shaft, which is the cheapest overload protection there is. They need no lubrication, tolerate dust, and are quick to replace. Their costs: some creep, a large shaft load from belt tension, and several belts of a matched set.

Chain drive: a chain is positive and stiff, so every shock goes straight into the shafts, bearings and motor, and a jam stalls the motor or breaks the weakest part unless a shear pin or slip clutch is added. In dust it needs a sealed case and an oil bath, or it wears fast. Its exact ratio and compactness are no advantage here.

answer.text: Comparison for this duty:

head: Criterion
V-belt
Chain
rows: Needs a shear pin or slip clutch
Needs a sealed case and oil

answer.text: Design consequence for the V-belt drive. With the B-section rating of the worked example (2.149 kW per belt after the arc and length factors), a 7.5 kW motor gives:
answer.pre:
smooth compressor, service factor 1.2:  P<sub>d</sub> = 9.0 kW   z = 9.0/2.149 = 4.19 → 5 belts
crusher, service factor 1.5:          P<sub>d</sub> = 11.25 kW  z = 11.25/2.149 = 5.24 → 6 belts

answer: So the shock duty costs one extra belt, a small price. If the count went above about 8, the designer would move to a larger section or larger pulleys.

Recommendation: a V-belt drive with a heavy-duty service factor (1.5 or more, from the maker’s table), a matched set of belts, an adjustable motor base for tensioning, and a belt guard. A flywheel on the crusher shaft, which crushers often carry, can serve as the large pulley.

When the chain would win: if the crusher were inside a hot, oily enclosure where rubber would perish, or if the shafts had to keep exact timing with another machine; then a chain with a shear-pin sprocket or a slip clutch would be used.
Check: 1.5 × 7.5 = 11.25 kW and 11.25/2.149 = 5.24, so 6 belts carry 6 × 2.149 = 12.9 kW ≥ 11.25 kW, while 5 belts would carry only 10.7 kW.

glossary.def: An endless flexible band that transmits power between two pulleys by friction.
A belt of rectangular cross-section that runs on a flat or slightly crowned pulley rim.
A belt of trapezoidal cross-section that wedges into a grooved pulley to gain extra friction.
A series of pin-jointed links, usually carrying rollers, that transmits power by engaging the teeth of two sprockets.
A toothed wheel whose teeth engage the chain rollers and so drive it without slip.
A grooved wheel over which a rope runs, used in hoists and rope drives.
A tension member made by twisting steel wires into strands and strands into a rope around a core.
A group of wires twisted together in a helix, several of which are laid up to form a wire rope.
The central member of a wire rope, of fibre or steel, that supports the strands and holds lubricant.
The helical pattern and direction in which wires and strands are twisted to form a rope.
The centre-to-centre distance between two adjacent chain rollers, measured along the chain.
The diameter of the circle on which the chain rollers or belt centre line sit when wrapped on the sprocket or pulley.
The arc of the pulley or sheave actually covered by the belt or rope; it is used in radians in the tension ratio.
The ratio of the limiting friction force to the normal reaction between belt and pulley.
The small relative motion between belt and pulley caused by unequal elastic stretch on the two sides.
Gross relative sliding between belt and pulley that occurs when the required friction exceeds the available friction.
The tension induced in a moving belt or rope by its own mass as it travels round the pulley.
A small extra pulley used to increase the angle of lap or to take up slack in a belt drive.
The periodic variation in chain speed caused by the chain wrapping a sprocket as a polygon rather than a circle.
The ratio of the failure load or stress to the working load or stress, applied to cover uncertainty and duty.
The tensile load at which a chain, rope or belt actually fractures in a pull test.
The included angle of a V-belt pulley groove, 34° to 38°, a little less than the 40° of the belt, which sets the wedging gain.
A multiplier applied to the transmitted power to account for the nature of the driven machine and its hours of duty.
The joint by which a flat belt is made endless, by lacing, metal fasteners, or cementing and vulcanising.
A rope lay in which the wires and the strands are twisted the same way; flexible and hard-wearing, but it tends to untwist under a free load.
Independent wire rope core: a small wire rope used as the core of a larger one, for strength and resistance to crushing.
